entities.name: Henry of Asti
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry of Asti (died 1345) stands as a pivotal, albeit ultimately tragic, figure in the Latin West's efforts to stem Ottoman expansion in the mid-14th century. Appointed titular Latin Catholic Patriarch of Constantinople in 1339 and serving concurrently as Bishop of Negroponte (modern-day Euboea) in Frankish Greece, Henry was a key papal legate tasked with galvanizing a fragmented Western presence in the Aegean. His significance is intrinsically tied to his leadership of the first Smyrniote Crusade (1342–45), a direct response to escalating Turkish piracy and the burgeoning power of the Aydinid emirate.

Commissioned by Pope Clement VI, Henry of Asti meticulously organized and led the naval coalition comprising forces from the Papacy, Venice, the Knights Hospitaller, and Cyprus. This formidable fleet achieved a decisive victory on October 28, 1344, capturing the lower city and harbor of Smyrna from Umur Bey, the Emir of Aydin. This strategic success temporarily secured a vital port for Christian shipping and trade in the eastern Aegean, dealing a significant blow to Turkish naval power. Henry, however, did not long enjoy this triumph; he perished on January 17, 1345, during a disastrous attempt to celebrate Mass in an abandoned church within the still-contested upper city, falling victim to a sudden Turkish counter-attack alongside other prominent crusader leaders.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry of Asti's leadership of the Smyrniote Crusade led to the temporary recapture of Smyrna, a critical port, from Turkish forces, demonstrating the potential for coordinated papal-led action against Ottoman expansion and influencing subsequent crusading efforts.
